title: How lovely are thy tabernacles (Psalm 83 [84])
hookLine: even the sparrow finds a home near the altar
tomorrow: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 89 [90])

cards: A weekday afternoon in an old stone church, and something is moving near the ceiling.
A sparrow flew in through an open door and now lives in the rafters, hopping along a beam above the altar, unbothered by the saints and the candles. People smile at it. The sexton sighs about it.
Long ago, a pilgrim walking into the Temple in Jerusalem noticed the same thing, a small bird nesting near the altar, and felt a stab of envy.

teach.b: Psalm 83 in the Douay, 84 in most Bibles, is a pilgrim's song: "How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord."
Tabernacles here means dwellings, the courts of the Temple. Fainteth: homesick to the point of weakness. Then the bird.
"For the sparrow hath found herself a house, and the turtle a nest for herself where she may lay her young ones: Thy altars, O Lord of hosts." The turtle is a turtledove.
Two small, ordinary birds get to live at the altar full time, while the pilgrim can only visit. It's funny and aching at once. Then the road.

Blessed are those whose strength is in you, the psalm says, who have set their hearts on the journey, and it names a valley they pass through. The Hebrew calls it the valley of Baca, a place scholars can't pin down.
The name may mean balsam trees, or weeping. The Latin read it as weeping, so the Douay says: "In the vale of tears."
Tradition traces the phrase vale of tears to this verse; it's the same valley of tears the Hail, Holy Queen sighs through. In the Hebrew, the pilgrims pass through it and make it a place of springs.

Then the well-known line: "For better is one day in thy courts above thousands." One day near God, better than a thousand anywhere else. Centuries later, Brahms set its opening lines in his German Requiem.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 83 [84] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, often on feasts of dedication of churches; some also make short visits to a church simply to sit in the quiet.

o: the nests the sparrow and the dove built
dwellings: the courts of God's house in Jerusalem
the pilgrims' rest stops along the road

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: a turtledove, nesting by the altar
the valley the pilgrims pass through

s: the turtle in this psalm is a reptile
it's a turtledove, nesting near the altar.
tradition traces the phrase vale of tears to this psalm's Latin
the Hebrew names the valley of Baca; the Latin read it as weeping.
the pilgrim in the psalm lives at the Temple full time
only the birds do. the pilgrim envies the sparrow.

games.q: you're a pilgrim walking into the Temple courts, and you see a sparrow nesting by the altar. how does the psalm feel about it?
o: envious and glad: even the sparrow has a home here.
games.why: the sparrow hath found herself a house. the smallest bird gets to live where the pilgrim can only visit.

practice: Sit somewhere quiet, a church if one is near, or the quietest corner you can find, even a parked car, and picture the sparrow on the beam, completely at home. Ask yourself where you feel that at home, and when you last were there.
If you pray, say how lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord; if you don't, let this quiet corner be a small place to rest.

wordCard.voice: Tabernacles. Dwellings, the courts of the Temple, the pilgrim's homesick song for God's house, where even the sparrow has a home. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: how lovely, how beloved, the psalm's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: the sparrow found a home. The pilgrim visits; the sparrow stays. Until tomorrow.
